title: Burnout: Signs, Recovery, and When It's Actually Depression
description: How to recognize burnout, distinguish it from depression, evidence-based recovery strategies, and when to seek professional help.

content.text: You're exhausted. Cynical. Checked out. Is it burnout or something more? Here's how to tell and what to do about it.
The WHO defines burnout as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress. Three dimensions:

items: Exhaustion: Feeling drained, depleted of energy
Cynicism: Mental distance from work, negativity, detachment
Reduced efficacy: Feeling incompetent, unproductive, like nothing you do matters

content.text: Key distinction: Burnout is tied to work context. Depression pervades all areas of life.

items: Energy improves on vacation/weekends (at least initially)

content.text: Prolonged burnout can evolve into depression. If symptoms persist after addressing work stressors, or extend beyond work life, seek professional evaluation.
Note: It's rarely just 'poor self-care.' Systemic workplace factors usually drive burnout.

items: Take whatever time off you can (even a mental health day)
Delegate or drop what you can
Consider whether the job is fixable

content.text: Burnout is real and serious, but it's not the same as depression. Recovery requires addressing the work factors driving it—not just 'self-care.' If rest and boundaries don't help, or symptoms extend beyond work, it may be depression, and professional help is warranted.
